prompt: Where in the system does IPsec protect traffic, compared with TLS?
hint: Applications do not know it is there.

choices.text: In the network stack, for every application
choices.why: Right: TLS lives inside one application's connection.

choices.text: Inside the browser, for HTTPS pages only
choices.why: That is TLS's usual place.

choices.text: In the DNS resolver, for name lookups
choices.why: That is DNSSEC's territory, and it signs rather than encrypts.

choices.text: In the mail client, per message
choices.why: That is S/MIME.

prompt: Vereda connects two clinics with a site-to-site VPN in tunnel mode. What does an observer on the internet between them see?
hint: The whole original packet is encrypted.

choices.text: Which workstations talk to which servers, but not the data
choices.why: Inner addresses are inside the encrypted part.

choices.text: The TCP ports in use, since ESP leaves them in clear
choices.why: Ports are inside the encrypted original packet.

choices.text: Only the two gateways exchanging ESP packets
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Nothing at all, not even that traffic exists
choices.why: Packet sizes and timing still show.

prompt: Which part of IPsec plays the role of lesson 7's authenticated key exchange?

choices.text: ESP
choices.why: ESP protects packets with keys it was given.

choices.text: AH
choices.why: AH authenticates packets; it agrees no keys.

choices.text: IKEv2
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The SPI
choices.why: The SPI only names an association.

prompt: What does DNSSEC protect a DNS answer against?

choices.text: Being read by somebody on the network
choices.why: Lookups stay visible; DNSSEC encrypts nothing.

choices.text: Being forged or altered
choices.why: Right: a forged answer fails validation.

choices.text: Being slow
choices.why: Signatures make answers larger, not faster.

choices.text: The zone's server going down
choices.why: That is availability, a different property.

prompt: Match each DNSSEC record to what it is.

pairs.right: a signature over a record set
a public key of the zone
the parent's hash of the child's KSK
signed proof that a name does not exist

prompt: The portal's address was changed in the signed zone without re-signing. Who notices, and when?

choices.text: The patient's browser, when it opens the portal
choices.why: Browsers do not validate DNSSEC themselves.

choices.text: A validating resolver, which returns a failure
choices.why: Right: users of non-validating resolvers get the forged address.

choices.text: The root zone, which refuses to serve it
choices.why: The root never sees the record.

choices.text: Nobody: DNSSEC only checks the DS record
choices.why: Every record set carries its own RRSIG.

prompt: What is the key tag of the zone signing key that signed the portal's A record?
Why is a voice call protected with SRTP instead of carrying the audio inside a TLS stream?
hint: What happens to a late audio packet?

choices.text: TLS cannot encrypt audio
choices.why: TLS encrypts any bytes.

choices.text: SRTP uses a stronger cipher than TLS
choices.why: Both use AES; strength is not the reason.

choices.text: Each packet must decrypt on its own, losses included
choices.why: Right: TLS assumes an ordered, reliable stream.

choices.text: Because VoIP runs over TCP
choices.why: RTP runs over UDP.

prompt: An old phone system uses SDES and sends its SIP signalling in clear text on port 5060. What follows?
hint: Where does SDES put the key?

choices.text: The calls are safe, because the media itself uses SRTP
choices.why: The SRTP key is readable in the signalling.

choices.text: Calls fail, because SRTP requires TLS on the media
choices.why: They work; that is the problem.

choices.text: Whoever reads the signalling has the media keys
choices.why: Right: SDES needs SIP over TLS, or DTLS-SRTP instead.

choices.text: Only the caller IDs are exposed
choices.why: The keys are exposed too.

prompt: Browser video calls use WebRTC, which makes ___-SRTP mandatory.
What does S/MIME protect that TLS between mail servers does not?
hint: Where is the message in clear text in each case?

choices.text: The message's headers
choices.why: Headers stay in clear in S/MIME too.

choices.text: The connection between the client and its server
choices.why: TLS already protects that hop.

choices.text: The message itself, in every server and mailbox
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The sender's IP address
choices.why: Neither hides that.

prompt: In the encrypted message, how is Bruno identified as the recipient?

choices.text: By his certificate's issuer and serial number
choices.why: Right: 23042 is 0x5A02.

choices.text: By his e-mail address in clear text
choices.why: The structure names the certificate, not the address.

choices.text: By a hash of his password
choices.why: Passwords play no part.

choices.text: He is not identified; anybody can try every key
choices.why: The recipient info names him.

prompt: Ana could not decrypt the message she had just encrypted to Bruno. How do mail clients keep the sent copy readable?
hint: The hybrid scheme allows several recipients.

choices.text: They keep the AES key in the sent folder in clear
choices.why: That would defeat the encryption.

choices.text: They store the plaintext and encrypt only in transit
choices.why: Then the server holds the message in clear.

choices.text: They add the sender as a second recipient
choices.why: Right: one more wrapped key, the same ciphertext.

choices.text: They encrypt with the sender's private key as well
choices.why: Private keys sign; they do not encrypt to anybody.

prompt: Match each protocol to what it protects.

pairs.right: IP packets between hosts or gateways
the media packets of a call

prompt: Which of these protocols ENCRYPT what they protect? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of the four only signs.

choices.text: IPsec with ESP
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: SRTP
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: DNSSEC
choices.why: No: it signs, and lookups stay visible.

choices.text: S/MIME used to encrypt
choices.why: Yes, when encryption is used, not only signing.
